Luciana, hi! Great news: our client loved the project summary you sent. The board approved the second phase yesterday.
That is wonderful, Ryan. Thank you. Actually, I wanted to talk about that. Today we are your subcontractor for one client. I was wondering if we could do more together.
Interesting. What do you have in mind?
You have more clients in your pipeline in Brazil. We could scale this model and present a joint offer. Would you be open to exploring that?
I like it, but that is a decision for our VP of Partnerships, Karen. She is visiting Brazil in November.
Perfect timing. How about setting up an executive meeting in São Paulo while she is here? It could be a win-win.
Let me check her calendar. She has two free mornings, the tenth and the twelfth.
The tenth works for us. I will follow up with an email today, with a short agenda.

I get about thirty meeting requests every week, and I accept maybe three. So what makes me say yes? Two things. First, a clear benefit for my company. Not synergies. That word says nothing. I want something concrete: you have five clients in your pipeline in Brazil, we already delivered for one of them, how about a joint offer for the other four? Second, a small next step. Don't ask me for a partnership in the first email. Ask me for forty-five minutes. Something like: I was wondering if we could meet when you are in Sao Paulo. That is easy to say yes to.

Five years ago, my company was a subcontractor for an American group. One project, one client, in Milan. The project went well, and I saw an opportunity. The Americans had other clients in Italy, and they did not know the local market. So I asked for a meeting with their director for Europe. I did not say, please give us more work. I said, would you be open to exploring a joint offer for three hospitals? It was a win-win: they had the technology, and we had the local team. The meeting was in Milan, it lasted forty minutes, and today we work together in four countries.

Many good conversations die after the call. Everybody says, great idea, let's talk again, and then nothing happens. My rule is simple: I follow up the same day, never the next week. And my follow-up email has only three lines. Line one: thank you for your time today. Line two: the idea in one sentence, for example, a joint offer for your clients in Brazil. Line three: the next step with a date, for example, how about meeting on the tenth, at ten? That is all. Three lines are easy to read on a phone, and easy to forward to the boss.
